doc.title: Reading a live MySQL: what to extract, and how
doc.p: Research for the first feature of every engine, MySQL first: open a schema from a saved connection and fill it from the database's own catalogs, its structure from information_schema and, when it is on, its usage from performance_schema. Reading a dump comes next, as its own feature; every other engine follows the same order with its own catalogs. Measured on MySQL 5.7.44, 8.0.46 and 8.4.13 in Docker (2026-11-24), checked against the manuals. The order and the versions are decided (decisions live-first and mysql-versions); the rest is what a design session decides from (see the end).

steps.item: The saved connection. A profile in the workspace (host, port, user, database, TLS), its secret in the operating system's keychain, never in the workspace, never seen by the agent (connections.xml). Tested in the five steps before anything is read.
Which databases. information_schema.SCHEMATA, the system ones (mysql, information_schema, performance_schema, sys) left out; the person picks.

The structure, per database: the catalog for names and attributes, SHOW CREATE for each object's exact DDL, read by the same reader as a dump, so a live read and a dump of the same database give the same schema (the engine does this today, engines/mysql/src/live.rs).
The statistics: rows, data and index size per table, as estimates, with their age.
The usage, when performance_schema is on: per table and per index reads and writes, and the queries by digest. Off, the schema is read without it and says so.
One import turn: everything read lands in the cortex and the engine's tables as one logged operation, undoable, with what was read, from where, when, and as which user.

section.title: The three versions

row.cell: end of life (October 2023), still widely run
the transactional data dictionary: catalog queries are views over it

section.p: What 8.0 added that the read needs, and 5.7 lacks: CHECK_CONSTRAINTS (5.7 parses a CHECK and ignores it), INNODB_TABLESPACES (5.7: INNODB_SYS_TABLESPACES), ST_SPATIAL_REFERENCE_SYSTEMS, ST_GEOMETRY_COLUMNS, VIEW_TABLE_USAGE and VIEW_ROUTINE_USAGE (what a view reads, without parsing it), COLUMN_STATISTICS (histograms), roles, invisible columns, functional indexes. 8.0 removed INNODB_SYS_*, INNODB_LOCKS and the status and variable tables of information_schema (now in performance_schema). 8.0 and 8.4 differ in the catalog only by TABLESPACES, gone in 8.4.
section.note: The engine today supports 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7 (engines/mysql/src/versions.rs), and its live read queries tables 5.7 does not have. Supporting 5.7 is engine work: its versions, what it lacks, and a live read that asks a 5.7 the 5.7 way.

section.title: The structure: how to read it

list.item: Always one database at a time, its name a constant (WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = ?). On 5.7 a catalog query without it scans the data directory and opens every table's files; with it, the server opens only that database's (5.7 manual). Joining TABLES to COLUMNS is about 30 times faster on 8.0 than 5.7 (MySQL blog): query each catalog table once per database and join in the engine, never in SQL.

The DDL from SHOW CREATE, as the server would write it, read by the dump reader: one reader, one truth. Measured with 1,000 tables, 5,000 columns, 5,000 indexes and 1,000 foreign keys in one database, one session: each catalog query 0.07 to 0.09 s on 8.4 and 0.12 to 0.27 s on 5.7 (emulated); 1,000 SHOW CREATE TABLE 0.3 s on both.

The catalog for what the DDL does not say: a view's definer and security, a routine's characteristics, a trigger's order, an event's schedule and status, and on 8.0 what a view reads (VIEW_TABLE_USAGE).
Read only. No ANALYZE TABLE, no FLUSH, no TRUNCATE of performance_schema: each writes or resets something the server's owner relies on.

section.title: The statistics: estimates, with their age
section.p: TABLE_ROWS, DATA_LENGTH, INDEX_LENGTH and CARDINALITY are InnoDB's estimates. On 8.0 and 8.4 they are also cached, for information_schema_stats_expiry seconds (one day by default), and a table never analysed can show NULL (8.0 manual, bug 86170). The read sets the session's expiry to 0 to ask InnoDB directly (slower, still read only), and keeps each number as an estimate with the time it was read; 5.7 asks InnoDB every time.

section.title: The usage: performance_schema
section.p: On by default in 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4 (SELECT @@performance_schema). On Amazon RDS it is on when Performance Insights manages it, and turning it on or off needs a reboot (AWS); a managed server may have it off, and the read never changes it.

row.cell: rows read, written, inserted, updated, deleted, and the time spent: hot and cold tables
reads per index (INDEX_NAME NULL: rows read without one): an index never read since the server started is a candidate to drop, never a verdict
each normalised statement: how often, rows examined against rows sent, no index used, temporary tables, sorts; 8.0 and 8.4 add the 95th, 99th and 99.9th percentile, CPU time and a sample of the text
time waited on each table's locks
every counter counts from the server's start: each read keeps the uptime, so two reads give a difference over a known time, and a restart between them shows

list.item: Measured: the same small workload on 5.7 and 8.4 gave the same counts per table, per index and per digest.

The digest table has a fixed size (performance_schema_digests_size); when it is full, new statements go to one row with no digest. The read says when that row is not empty: the query list is then incomplete.

The base tables, not sys: sys is views over them (present on all three here), may be missing on a managed server, and its views change between versions. What sys.schema_unused_indexes and sys.schema_redundant_indexes say, the engine works out from the base tables and the structure it read.

section.title: The account: least privilege, tested

cell.c: SELECT, SHOW VIEW, TRIGGER, EVENT ON db.*

row.cell: 5.7: without it a routine not defined by the account is invisible (tested: PROCEDURE does not exist)
routine bodies; without it ROUTINE_DEFINITION is NULL (8.4 manual)

section.p: The Connections page shows these grants for the server's version, and the connection test's last step says which are missing and what will be read without them.

section.title: For the design session

list.item: Versions: decided (decision mysql-versions): 5.7, 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7; the engine work that adds 5.7, and its live read the 5.7 way, is a task to write.

Where the usage is kept: snapshots per table, index and digest, each with the server's uptime and the time read, in the cortex (shared by every engine: rows, reads, writes, size) and the engine's tables (what only MySQL measures); decision insight-layer.

The version facts, as data: what each version has and lacks (its types, kinds of object, options, catalog tables and grants, the facts this research measured), kept as rows of the engine's tables, one per version and feature, so the agent can ask them: design for a target version, plan an upgrade (what changes from 5.7 to 8.0 or 8.4 for this schema), check a schema meant for several versions, and read usage beside them. The engine's code holds these facts today (engines/mysql/src/versions.rs); the session decides their tables and how they stay one source.
When it is read: on opening, on demand, and on a schedule while the app runs, each a snapshot, never a reset.

The other engines: each declares its catalog for the structure and its source for the usage (PostgreSQL: pg_catalog and pg_stat_user_tables, pg_stat_user_indexes, pg_stat_statements; Iceberg: its catalog and metadata files), so the shared part of the flow names none of them.

section.p: Test servers for this work, local only: sf-mysql-5-7 on 127.0.0.1:33057, sf-mysql-8-0 on 33080, sf-mysql-8-4 on 33084, sf-mysql-9-7 on 33097 (Docker, restarting with Docker).
